newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New tea image urged to attract young consumers.
newsitem.headline: New tea image urged to attract young consumers.

text.p: Tea needs to discard its staid image and should be marketed liked a soft drink, to attract younger consumers in the face of rising world output and stagnant demand, industry officials said on Tuesday.
"I feel we have to market tea that way," Ranjith Maligaspe, director-general of the Sri Lanka Tea Board, told Reuters in an interview on the last day of an Asia Tea Industry conference in Singapore.
"Tea has been identified as a drink of the older generation. I think we should target the younger generation," he added.

"Tea has a very stodgy image while colas have a very macho image. The younger generation today drinks colas for breakfast," a member of India's Tata Group told delegates discussing how to expand tea markets beyond the year 2000.
The official added the tea industry should take its cue from beverage giants Coca-Cola and PepsiCo in how they aggressively position their product for young people around the world.
Maligaspe said it was vital for tea to develop new markets because global production is rising while consumption may remain at a standstill.
"By the year 2000, world supply of tea will exceed demand," he said.

Production expansion programmes in many countries would boost output to 2.81 million tonnes by the year 2005 from the 1991-93 average of 1.91 million tonnes, the United Nations body the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) told the conference.
But tea imports by major consumers like Britain dropped nearly eight percent in 1995 to 137,000 tonnes while U.S. imports slid 15.8 percent to 81,300 tonnes, the FAO said.
"I think the carbonated drinks market is one area we can target," Maligaspe said, adding "prices could go down" if producers fail to market the excess tea or develop new markets.
Tea producers should promote the beverage as a health drink when compared with soft drinks while discarding its persistent image as a hot drink, another delegate said.
Tea producers should also develop markets in the Asia Pacific region, Eastern Europe and the former republics of the Soviet Union, Maligaspe said.
The world's major producers of tea are Sri Lanka, India, Malaysia, Kenya, China, Malawi and Bangladesh.
